question: Compared with a laminar boundary layer, a turbulent boundary layer:

options.text: Has less kinetic energy near the surface and separates more easily
Produces less skin friction drag but separates more easily
Has more kinetic energy near the surface and resists separation better, at the cost of higher skin friction drag
Is unaffected by surface roughness or airflow speed

explanation: A turbulent boundary layer mixes energetic outer airflow down toward the surface, giving it more kinetic energy than a smooth laminar layer. This makes it more resistant to separation and stall, but the extra mixing also raises skin friction drag compared with laminar flow.

question: The "transition point" on an aerofoil surface is where:

options.text: The boundary layer changes from laminar to turbulent flow
The airflow separates completely from the surface
The center of pressure is located
A shockwave forms in transonic flight

explanation: The transition point marks where the initially laminar boundary layer, starting at the leading edge, becomes turbulent. Its position moves forward as speed or surface roughness increases, and aft on a wing specifically shaped to hold laminar flow longer.

question: Boundary layer separation occurs when:

options.text: The boundary layer's kinetic energy is overcome by an adverse (rising) pressure gradient, and it can no longer follow the surface's contour
The airflow becomes too fast for the surface
The aircraft descends below its minimum safe altitude
Dynamic pressure drops to zero everywhere

explanation: As airflow moves aft over the rear portion of an aerofoil, pressure rises (an adverse pressure gradient). If the boundary layer's remaining kinetic energy cannot overcome that rising pressure, it separates from the surface, reversing direction locally and leaving turbulent, disorganised flow behind it.

question: When the boundary layer separates from the upper surface of a wing at high angle of attack, the immediate effect is:

options.text: A sharp increase in lift and a decrease in drag
A sharp loss of lift and a sharp increase in drag — the aerodynamic definition of a stall
No measurable change in either lift or drag
An increase in critical Mach number

explanation: Widespread boundary layer separation over the upper surface is, in aerodynamic terms, exactly what a stall is: the organised airflow that produced most of the wing's lift is lost, lift falls sharply, and pressure drag rises sharply as the separated wake widens.

question: Small vortex generators fitted to a wing's upper surface work by:

options.text: Reducing skin friction drag directly
Energising the boundary layer by mixing high-energy outer airflow into it, delaying separation
Increasing the wing's aspect ratio
Reducing the wing's angle of incidence

explanation: Vortex generators are small fins angled to the local airflow that shed tiny trailing vortices, mixing energetic air from outside the boundary layer down into it. This re-energised boundary layer resists an adverse pressure gradient for longer, delaying separation to a higher angle of attack.

question: A small "stall strip" fitted to the leading edge, near the wing root, is designed to:

options.text: Delay the stall at the root so the wingtip stalls first
Deliberately trigger earlier local separation at the root, ensuring the root stalls before the tip does
Increase the critical Mach number
Reduce induced drag

explanation: A stall strip is a small, deliberately placed leading-edge disruption that provokes earlier boundary layer separation at the wing root. It is one way of ensuring root-first stall progression (keeping the ailerons effective longer) on a wing whose planform alone does not provide enough natural washout.

question: Surface contamination such as frost, insect residue, or paint roughness on a wing's leading edge tends to:

options.text: Delay transition to turbulent flow, improving performance
Promote earlier transition to turbulent flow and can promote earlier separation, degrading CLmax
Have no effect on the boundary layer
Only matter at supersonic speed

explanation: Roughness disturbs the boundary layer, tripping it into turbulence earlier than it would transition on a clean, smooth surface, and can also promote earlier separation. This is why even light frost on a wing can measurably raise stalling speed and reduce climb performance.

question: Some high-lift systems use "boundary layer control" by blowing high-pressure air over the wing or flap surface. Its purpose is to:

options.text: Re-energise the boundary layer so it resists separation at a higher lift coefficient/angle of attack
Cool the wing surface
Reduce fuel consumption directly
Increase the critical Mach number

explanation: Blowing high-energy air over the surface reinjects kinetic energy into the boundary layer, letting it withstand a stronger adverse pressure gradient before separating. This allows a higher usable lift coefficient than the same surface could achieve unaided.

question: A "laminar flow" wing section is shaped to keep the boundary layer laminar over as much of the chord as possible, mainly to:

options.text: Increase CLmax at low speed
Reduce skin friction drag at cruise, since a laminar boundary layer produces less friction than a turbulent one
Improve stall characteristics
Increase the stalling angle of attack

explanation: Laminar flow sections move the point of peak suction, and therefore the natural transition point, further aft, holding the low-friction laminar boundary layer over more of the chord to reduce cruise drag. The trade-off is that such sections can have less benign, more abrupt stall characteristics than a conventional section.

question: Reynolds number is a dimensionless value used to characterise a flow, broadly comparing:

options.text: Inertial forces to viscous forces in the airflow, which affects where transition and separation occur
Lift to drag, at a given angle of attack
True airspeed to the speed of sound
Altitude to air temperature

explanation: Reynolds number compares inertial forces to viscous forces in a flow. A higher Reynolds number (larger scale, higher speed) generally favours earlier transition to turbulent flow, which is one reason boundary layer behaviour observed on a small wind-tunnel model does not scale directly to a full-size aircraft.

question: A "favourable" pressure gradient, found over the forward part of a typical aerofoil where airflow is still accelerating, is one in which:

options.text: Pressure falls in the direction of flow, helping to keep the boundary layer attached
Pressure rises sharply in the direction of flow
Pressure remains completely constant
Airflow is always turbulent

explanation: Where airflow is still accelerating over the forward part of an aerofoil, static pressure falls in the direction of flow — a favourable gradient that tends to keep the boundary layer thin, energetic and firmly attached, in contrast to the adverse (rising-pressure) gradient found further aft.

question: On a typical subsonic aerofoil below the stall, the adverse pressure gradient is generally most severe:

options.text: At the leading edge stagnation point
Toward the rear of the aerofoil, where pressure is recovering back toward the freestream value
Nowhere — subsonic aerofoils have no adverse pressure gradient at all
Only at supersonic speed

explanation: After accelerating over the point of maximum suction (usually well forward on the upper surface), airflow must decelerate and its pressure must rise back toward the freestream value as it approaches the trailing edge. This rear portion is where the adverse pressure gradient is strongest, and therefore where separation is most likely to begin.

subtopic: Spanwise Flow on a Swept Wing
question: On a swept wing, the boundary layer tends to drift spanwise, outboard toward the tip, mainly because:

options.text: The pressure distribution on a swept wing has a spanwise component that carries the slow-moving boundary layer air outboard
Engine exhaust pushes it outward
The ailerons force it outward
Sweepback has no effect on boundary layer direction

explanation: Sweep introduces a spanwise component to the pressure field over the wing, and because the slow-moving air deep in the boundary layer is more easily redirected than the faster air outside it, this drift accumulates a thickened, energy-depleted boundary layer toward the tip — a major contributor to a swept wing's natural tendency to stall tip-first.

question: A "wing fence" — a small, chord-wise fixed vane on the upper surface of a swept wing — is fitted mainly to:

options.text: Block the spanwise drift of the boundary layer toward the tip, helping to delay tip stall
Increase the wing's critical Mach number
Reduce skin friction drag
Act as a lightning conductor

explanation: By physically interrupting the spanwise flow of the outboard-drifting boundary layer on a swept wing, a wing fence keeps more of that flow attached over the tip region for longer, helping ensure the root stalls well before the tip and preserving aileron control into the early stages of a stall.

question: A "vortilon" — a small vane mounted under the wing's leading edge, ahead of the fence position — works by:

options.text: Generating a small trailing vortex that helps re-energise the upper-surface boundary layer outboard of it, delaying tip stall
Reducing engine noise
Directly increasing wing area
Cooling the wing structure

explanation: Mounted beneath the leading edge, a vortilon sheds a small vortex that trails back over the upper surface outboard of it, mixing energy into the boundary layer there — a similar tip-stall-delaying purpose to a wing fence, but achieved by energising the flow rather than simply blocking its spanwise drift.

question: A plain (unslotted) trailing-edge flap generally has a much lower maximum usable deflection angle than a slotted flap, mainly because:

options.text: Beyond a fairly modest angle, the boundary layer over the flap's upper surface separates, and further deflection adds little useful lift
Plain flaps are structurally weaker than slotted flaps
Plain flaps have no maximum deflection limit at all
Slotted flaps cannot be deflected as far as plain flaps

explanation: With no slot to re-energise it, the boundary layer over a plain flap's upper surface separates once the flap is deflected beyond a relatively modest angle, so deflecting it further adds mostly drag rather than lift. A slotted flap's re-energised boundary layer resists this separation, allowing a considerably larger, more useful deflection angle.

question: A "leading-edge stall", typical of aerofoils with a fairly sharp leading edge, is characterised by:

options.text: Gradual separation starting at the trailing edge and creeping forward well before the stalling angle is reached
An abrupt, sudden separation right at the leading edge once the critical angle of attack is reached, with little warning
A stall that only occurs at supersonic speed
No change in lift coefficient at all

explanation: On aerofoils with a relatively sharp leading edge, the boundary layer there is already under considerable strain at high angle of attack, and separation at the leading edge tends to be sudden and complete rather than gradual — producing an abrupt loss of lift with comparatively little pre-stall buffet warning.

question: A "trailing-edge stall", typical of aerofoils with a well-rounded, generous leading edge, is characterised by:

options.text: Separation beginning at the trailing edge and progressively creeping forward as angle of attack increases, giving a gradual, gentle stall with good warning
A sudden, total loss of lift with the first sign of separation happening at the leading edge
A stall that produces no buffet whatsoever
A stall unrelated to boundary layer behaviour

explanation: A generous leading-edge radius keeps the leading-edge boundary layer robust even at high angle of attack, so separation instead begins at the trailing edge, where the adverse pressure gradient is strongest, and creeps forward gradually — producing a gentler stall with progressive buffet and better aerodynamic warning than a leading-edge stall.

question: A "thin-aerofoil stall", associated with very thin sections at low Reynolds number, involves:

options.text: A small separation bubble forming right at the sharp leading edge at a fairly low angle of attack, which then bursts as angle of attack increases further
Separation that always begins at the trailing edge only
A stall that only affects thick, generously rounded aerofoils
No separation bubble of any kind

explanation: On very thin sections, a small laminar separation bubble tends to form near the sharp leading edge even at a modest angle of attack. As angle of attack increases, this bubble can suddenly burst rather than simply growing, producing a distinct third stall mechanism alongside the classic leading-edge and trailing-edge stall types.

question: Testing the same aerofoil shape at a much lower Reynolds number than a full-size aircraft normally experiences (as on a small model) generally:

options.text: Increases the achievable maximum lift coefficient
Tends to reduce the achievable maximum lift coefficient, since the boundary layer separates more readily at low Reynolds number
Has no effect on maximum lift coefficient at all
Only affects drag, never lift

explanation: At low Reynolds number, the boundary layer carries relatively less kinetic energy and separates more readily, generally reducing the maximum lift coefficient an aerofoil can achieve compared with the same shape at the higher Reynolds number a full-size aircraft experiences — a key reason small-scale wind-tunnel results need correction before being applied to a real aircraft.

question: A "separation bubble" (or "dead air" region) on an aerofoil surface refers to:

options.text: A region where the flow separates from the surface but then reattaches further downstream, enclosing a pocket of slow, recirculating air
A region of supersonic flow found only above the critical Mach number
The wingtip vortex itself
A permanent feature that never reattaches

explanation: Rather than separating permanently, the boundary layer can separate briefly, transition to turbulent flow within the separated region, and then reattach further downstream, enclosing a bubble of slow-moving, recirculating "dead air" between the separation and reattachment points — a distinct, more localised phenomenon than full separation.

question: "Active" laminar flow control, using suction through a perforated or porous wing skin, aims to:

options.text: Remove the slower, energy-depleted part of the boundary layer, delaying transition to turbulent flow further than the wing's shape alone would achieve
Blow high-pressure air outward through the skin to increase lift
Heat the wing surface to prevent ice
Increase skin friction drag deliberately

explanation: By drawing off the slow-moving, low-energy air nearest the surface through tiny perforations, suction-based laminar flow control keeps the remaining boundary layer thinner and more resistant to the instabilities that trigger transition, holding laminar (low-friction) flow over more of the surface than shaping alone could achieve — an "active" system, unlike a passive laminar-flow aerofoil shape.

question: Heavy rain on a wing's upper surface can degrade aerodynamic performance partly because it:

options.text: Forms a rough, disturbed water film that can thicken the boundary layer and promote earlier separation, reducing CLmax
Always increases the critical angle of attack
Has no aerodynamic effect until it freezes
Only affects the tailplane, never the wing

explanation: A disturbed film of water, and the impact of individual raindrops, roughens the effective surface and can add momentum loss to the boundary layer, promoting earlier separation and a measurable reduction in maximum lift coefficient — a genuine performance penalty in very heavy rain, distinct from any icing effect.

question: On some aircraft with an engine intake mounted close to the fuselage, a "boundary layer diverter" — a wedge-shaped gap or plate ahead of the intake — is fitted to:

options.text: Divert the slow-moving, turbulent fuselage boundary layer away from the intake, so the engine ingests cleaner, undisturbed air
Increase the fuselage's skin friction drag deliberately
Cool the engine compressor
Act as a lightning conductor

explanation: The fuselage's own boundary layer is slow, turbulent and uneven by the time it reaches an intake mounted close behind it. A diverter physically separates this degraded air from the intake's capture area, letting the engine draw in smoother, more uniform air and improving both efficiency and compressor stability.

question: As Reynolds number increases (for example, as airspeed increases), the skin friction drag coefficient of a given surface generally:

options.text: Increases, even though total skin friction drag force also increases with speed
Decreases, even though total skin friction drag force still increases with speed
Remains exactly constant at every Reynolds number
Is undefined for turbulent flow

explanation: The skin friction drag coefficient itself actually falls as Reynolds number rises, for both laminar and turbulent flow. Total skin friction drag force still increases with speed regardless, because the drag equation's dynamic pressure term (proportional to the square of speed) rises faster than the coefficient falls.

question: Along the chord of an aerofoil, from the leading edge stagnation point to the trailing edge, the boundary layer:

options.text: Starts at its maximum thickness and thins continuously toward the trailing edge
Starts at essentially zero thickness at the stagnation point and grows continuously thicker toward the trailing edge
Has a constant, unchanging thickness along the whole chord
Only exists over the aft half of the aerofoil

explanation: The boundary layer begins at essentially zero thickness right at the stagnation point, where the flow is brought to rest, and grows progressively thicker as it moves aft, since viscosity keeps slowing more of the flow near the surface the further it travels across the surface.

question: A "Gurney flap" — a small, right-angled tab fitted along the trailing edge of a wing or aerofoil — increases lift mainly by:

options.text: Altering the flow pattern right at the trailing edge, effectively increasing the aerofoil's aft camber and creating a small, stabilising pair of vortices behind it
Acting exactly like a large trailing-edge flap, but with a bigger deflection angle
Reducing the wing's angle of attack
Delaying transition to turbulent flow at the leading edge

explanation: Despite its small size — often just a centimetre or two tall — a Gurney flap changes the pressure distribution right at the trailing edge, effectively adding aft camber and generating a small, stabilising vortex pair immediately behind it, producing a worthwhile lift increase for very little added drag or complexity.

question: Near the top of the lift-versus-angle-of-attack curve, many aerofoils show the curve gradually rounding off rather than rising in a perfectly straight line right up to an abrupt peak. This rounding is caused by:

options.text: Growing regions of boundary layer separation developing progressively before the full stall is reached
A sudden increase in air density near the stall
The onset of compressibility effects, even at low speed
A change in the direction of the relative airflow

explanation: As angle of attack approaches the critical angle, small regions of the boundary layer begin separating even before the wing fully stalls, progressively reducing how much extra lift each further increment of angle of attack produces. This is what rounds off the top of the lift curve, rather than it rising in a straight line right up to a sharp peak followed by an instantaneous drop.
